items.title: Inkling 2 Mini is "Local Opus"?
items.summary:
Join this channel to get access to perks:
https://www.youtube.com/channel/@aicodeking/join

In this video, I'll cover the Inkling 2 Mini launch, how its looped transformer reuses layers, what it takes to run on a 32 GB Mac, and what OpenRouter charges. I'll walk through the Artificial Analysis results and coding benchmarks, then explain why I skipped KingBench 4 for a model this size. I'll time the same cache fix at low, medium, and high reasoning effort. Then I'll show how it handled five jobs I'd give a local model: patching Python, calling tools, fixing SQLite queries, writing a log CLI, and building a regex inspector. I ran them on OpenRouter for about 3 cents across all tests and retries, and I'll close with the jobs I'd trust it with and the fixes I'd double-check.

Links:
Thinking Machines Lab launch post: https://thinkingmachines.ai/news/inkling-2-mini/
Hugging Face model card: https://huggingface.co/thinkingmachines/Inkling-2-Mini
Unsloth GGUF downloads: https://huggingface.co
items.author: AICodeKing
items.transcript: [music] >> Hi. Welcome to another video. So yesterday, November [music] 20, 2026, Thinking Machines Lab released Inkling 2 Mini that came right after Inkling 2 Small, which has 594 billion parameters. This time, you get Apache 2.0 open weights and a model built to run on a Mac with 32 GB of memory. So what is Inkling 2 Mini actually like to use on real local developer tasks? First, let's look at how Inkling 2 Mini actually works and what it takes to run it. It's a loop transformer, which means it can send each token back through part of the same network. A token is a chunk of text the model reads or writes. It stores 24 layers and runs the middle 12 three times with the same weights. So you get 48 layer passes per token without storing 48 layers. That's 26.4 billion parameters in total. 3.4 billion active on a base pass and about 5.4 billion effective active parameters when you count the repeated work. It takes text and images directly and supports up to 1 million tokens of context, which is how much it can take into account at once. The official mixed precision checkpoint is 19.5 GB. Unsloth's 4-bit GGUF, a smaller package for local inference, is 17.6 GB. Thinking Machines recommends an Apple Silicon Mac with at least 32 GB of unified memory or a single NVIDIA DGX Spark. You can use Ollama, MLX, llama.cpp, or LM Studio. For Ollama, type Ollama run then Inkling-2-Mini. Inkling 2 Small meanwhile has 17 billion active parameters and takes about 354 GB at 4-bit. That's still a data center model for most of us. On Open Router, Prime Intellect charges 10 cents per million input tokens and 40 cents per million output tokens. Cached input costs 2 cents per million when the provider reuses part of the prompt. io.net lists 8 cents for input and 35 cents for output. Open Router caps the output at about 65,000 tokens. Now let's check the benchmarks and talk about why I did not run it on King Bench 4. Inkling 2 Mini scores 20.1 on Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index tied with Qwen 3.8 27 B. On that hosted benchmark, it generated 280 tokens per second and averaged 9 minutes and 59 cents per task. Qwen took 38 minutes and cost $3.53 cents per task. So the mini finished roughly four times faster and cost about 1/6 as much. Thinking Machines reports 79.2% on Sweet Bench verified and 77.9% on the hard split of Sweet Bench Pro version two. It gets 48.2% on Deep Sweet, 71.6% on Terminal Bench 2.1 and 46.5% on the Valse Index. Nan Beige 4.3 33 B is slightly ahead on the overall index at 20.4 and posts higher scores on some of its own test setups. King Bench 4 gives Frontier Models six full projects with one prompt each and no follow-up fixes. There's a Rust Game Boy and 3DS emulator, a Docker alternative, a 3D room designer, a QMK keyboard configurator, Pokémon Red, and a Fitbit desktop app. Even Claude Fable 5.2 at 42 out of 60, Gemini 4 Neon at 37.9 and Opus 5.5 at 34.7 still left bugs behind. A one-shot 3DS emulator tells me very little about how a model with 3.4 billion active parameters per base pass will fix my Python. So I used Open Router to test the work I'd actually give a local model. Before the tasks, let's talk about what using Inkling 2 Mini actually feels like. I used the Prime Intellect FP4 endpoint which runs the model at 4-bit precision. All 19 requests together cost about 3 cents. My requests defaulted to high reasoning and the model often spent 3,000 to 5,000 thinking tokens before it wrote a line of code. With output caps of 4,000 for Sequel, 5,000 for the command line tool, and 8,000 for the interface, all three first attempts hit the limit. So I gave it the exact same 5,353 token bug report at low, medium, and high effort. The cache stores results for reuse, but it gave the same result for requests for different fields. All three settings fixed it and passed all nine checks. Low finished in four seconds with 481 thinking tokens and cost under a tenth of a cent. Medium took 10.1 seconds with 1,903 thinking tokens. High took 15.4 seconds with 3,823. I'd start on lower medium for everyday work and save high for a really hard bug. Now let's go through the five local tasks I ran on it, starting with Python and tool calling. First was a Python rate limiter which decides how many requests can get through in a moving window of time. I planted an off by one error at the window boundary, mixed timestamps with and without time zones, and left a gap where two threads could update the counter at once. It fixed all three and got six out of seven checks in 12.2 seconds for under two tenths of a cent. In my race check, the fixed code let just one of 16 simultaneous requests through. The broken version let all 16 through. Its own pay test tests passed, but they still passed when I took the lockout. I'd want an independent concurrency test before relying on that patch. Then I tested tool calling where the model asks a program to run a function and gets the result back. In auto mode, it called read config, list endpoints, and the schema validator in parallel with the exact arguments on the first turn. On the second turn, it returned a migration plan in strict JSON with every required field and value in the right place. That was eight out of eight in 4.1 seconds. When I set tool choice to required, it only called read config and left the endpoint and validator lists empty. That felt a five out of eight. I checked both modes before wiring it into an agent. Next, I tested it on SQLite analytics debugging and a zero dependency log tool. The SQLite database had 561 rows. The revenue query joined orders, items, and refunds in a way that counted the same money more than once. The fix matched all 16 days to the cent, including $26,988 cents on February 1st. It also fixed a not in subquery that gave the wrong answer when it saw a missing value and found all 21 churned customers. The catch was the seven day rolling total. It built the January calendar, then filtered for February in the same select that calculated the window. That dropped January's counts from six dates, so February one came back as three when it should have been 25. It finished in 16.1 seconds with six out of seven checks. Log peak runs without extra packages and reads JSONL, which puts one JSON record on each line. I gave it 200 lines with 159 valid objects, 32 broken records, and nine blanks. JSON output, case insensitive dash dash level, cross midnight dash dash since literal grep and top error ranking all worked. It sent warnings about broken lines to standard error and returned the right exit codes for bad flags. It scored 10 out of 12 in 26.4 seconds. Both misses came from one line. It used dot lower instead of dot case fold, so uppercase strass and missed the German word strasse with an SZ. For the fifth task, I wanted to see how it handles a focused front-end utility. I asked for a macOS style regex tester and match inspector in one HTML file with CSS and JavaScript. A regex is a pattern you can use to find parts of a string. This is the sort of tool I'd actually keep open on my desktop, and it nailed it. It highlighted matches as I typed and put the pieces captured by each group into a table. The G I N M toggles and the email, URL, and ISO date presets all worked. It handled matches that consumed no characters and recovered when I entered a broken pattern. The layout fit desktop and mobile with zero JavaScript errors and zero external requests. That's 11 out of 11 in 37.5 seconds for about 4/10 of a cent. So, stepping back, what is my honest verdict on Inkling Too Many? For about 3 cents across every test and retry, I got good single-file fixes, reliable tool calls in auto mode, structured JSON, and a utility I'd use. Keep an eye on high effort if you have a tight output cap and double-check generated concurrency tests, SQL window filters, and Unicode searches. A giant one-shot King Bench 4 app is still a job I'd give to a much larger model. If you have a 32 GB Mac and want fast private help, the Apache 2.0 weights make it worth trying at low or medium effort. And if you already run an agent through Open Router, 10 cents per million input tokens makes it a cheap worker for focused tasks. Overall, it's pretty cool. Anyway, let me know your thoughts in the comments. If you liked this video, consider donating through the Super Thanks option or becoming a member by clicking [music] the Join button. Also, give this video a thumbs up and subscribe to my channel. I'll see you in the next one. Until then, bye.
